title: Episode 91: Reddit Trending — “It’s Like You’re Trying to Defuse a Bomb”: Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men’s Sexual Lives
itunes_title: Reddit Trending — “It’s Like You’re Trying to Defuse a Bomb”: Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men’s Sexual Lives
description:
**Top Trending Friday** — our weekly pick of the top-trending paper on r/science this week.

**["It's Like You're Trying to Defuse a Bomb": Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men's Sexual Lives](https://doi.org/10.1080/0092623X.2026.2740624)**

*Journal of Sex & Marital Therapy, 2026*

DOI: [10.1080/0092623X.2026.2740624](https://doi.org/10.1080/0092623X.2026.2740624)

**Question:** How do young heterosexual men, raised amid consent-focused sex education, emotionally experience sex?

**Answer:** In 31 interviews, most men spontaneously described anxiety, fear of causing harm, and shame — including self-directed shame — rather than enjoyment. The interview guide focused on uncertain/non-consensual encounters, so these counts describe this volunteer cohort, not prevalence.

**Three takeaways**

1. 29/31 men described anxiety and vigilance, 29/31 fear of harming a partner, 26/31 shame — themes heavily overlapped.
2. The distinctive pattern was inward: several men judged themselves, not just their partner's wishes, as the uncertain, risky object.
3. These are spontaneous-mention counts from self-selected men at one Australian university, not a prevalence estimate — the authors say so explicitly.

source_metadata.title: “It’s Like You’re Trying to Defuse a Bomb”: Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men’s Sexual Lives
source_metadata.abstract: This study examines how this generation of young heterosexual men-who have come of age in the "age of consent"-emotionally experience sex. We thematically analyzed 31 in-depth interviews with men aged 18 to 32 years. The most striking finding is how rarely these men described enjoying sex. Three themes emerged. First, anxiety and vigilance accompanied sexual encounters. Second, there was a moral concern about causing harm to a sexual partner. Third, shame arose not only from accusations by others, but also from self-criticism. The themes overlap substantially, suggesting aspects of a complex, sometimes contradictory experience. The defining feature is an inward turn: a cultural suspicion of men appears to have been internalized by some young men. For these men, the question when navigating consent is often not only "does she want this?" but "am I the kind of man who could get this wrong?" Sex, as one participant put it, is "like you're trying to defuse a bomb." These young men have come to approach sex as a hazard to manage rather than a relational experience to share. They attributed this wariness to the cultural climate that surrounds consent. We consider implications for consent education, clinical practice, and future research.
